source_metadata.title: SKILLER: Language-Level Reinforcement Learning for Reusable Skill Extraction in Small Language Models

atoms.canonical_statement: The study proposes SKILLER to automatically generate and refine executor-specific natural-language skills for compact language-model agents.
SKILLER treats the textual skill, rather than compact-model weights, as the optimizable policy and keeps the compact executor frozen.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: without updating the parameters of the compact model itself

atoms.canonical_statement: The environment wraps benchmark tools, workspace, and the official verifier around the compact model and returns an execution trajectory, scalar reward, and verifier diagnostics.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: invokes the official verifier to obtain the scalar reward

atoms.canonical_statement: At each step the optimization state is the quadruple of task instance, current trajectory, reference trajectory, and verifier diagnostics; the reward is binary success or normalized test pass rate when partial credit exists.
The critic contrasts the current trajectory with a successful reference, identifies the earliest causal divergence, and emits localized natural-language skill-modification suggestions.

Replay memory stores failure signatures with diagnostics, critic summaries, and accepted edits with outcomes, supplying prior evidence to later critic and actor steps and supporting retention or rollback.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: retains three forms of reusable evidence

atoms.canonical_statement: The actor applies bounded Insert, Replace, Create, or Delete edits, preserves effective content, and may synthesize deterministic task-local helper scripts.
A successful reference trajectory is privileged optimization evidence but is not provided to the compact model at runtime, and reference evidence is not inserted as a precomputed answer.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: never introduced as a direct runtime dependency

atoms.canonical_statement: The evaluation uses Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-4B as compact executors in the OpenCode agent loop and GPT-5.4 only during offline skill generation as actor and critic; compact-model evaluation tokens are excluded from reported generation cost.
The SkillsBench evaluation uses 26 tasks selected because each can be solved using a single skill.
The SWE-Skills-Bench evaluation uses 10 selected tasks comprising 117 instances where the original benchmark reports that adding a skill changes performance.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: This criterion yields 10 tasks and 117 instances

atoms.canonical_statement: SkillLearnBench is evaluated using its official configuration across 100 verified task instances.
GAIA evaluation covers 165 validation-set tasks; stratified skill generation uses 83 instances and the remaining 82 form the zero-shot test split.
EarthBench evaluation covers 248 samples; stratified skill generation uses 124 instances and the remaining 124 form the zero-shot test split.
Main reported benchmark results are averages over three executions of the same skill, and the main experimental setup states a five-step SKILLER reinforcement-learning schedule across tasks.

The abstract reports absolute gains of 4.3-20.4 percentage points for Qwen3.5-9B and 1.8-13.3 points for Qwen3.5-4B over compared skill-generation/evolution methods, while claiming near-frontier single-skill SkillsBench performance.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: absolute gains ranging from 4.3 to 20.4 percentage points

atoms.canonical_statement: On Qwen3.5-9B for SkillsBench, SKILLER scored 73.91% versus SkillX at 60.87%, a calculated difference of +13.04 percentage points.
On Qwen3.5-9B for SkillLearnBench, SKILLER scored 32.11% versus Human-authored at 30.00%, a calculated difference of +2.11 percentage points.
On Qwen3.5-9B for SWE-Skills-Bench, SKILLER scored 82.80% versus Manus at 62.40%, a calculated difference of +20.40 percentage points.
On Qwen3.5-9B for GAIA, SKILLER scored 49.40% versus SkillX at 49.40%, a calculated difference of +0.00 percentage points.
On Qwen3.5-9B for EarthBench, SKILLER scored 76.08% versus AutoSkill at 71.77%, a calculated difference of +4.31 percentage points.
On Qwen3.5-4B for SkillsBench, SKILLER scored 42.03% versus SkillX at 43.48%, a calculated difference of -1.45 percentage points.
On Qwen3.5-4B for SkillLearnBench, SKILLER scored 33.00% versus Manus at 31.17%, a calculated difference of +1.83 percentage points.
On Qwen3.5-4B for SWE-Skills-Bench, SKILLER scored 66.70% versus Manus at 53.40%, a calculated difference of +13.30 percentage points.
On Qwen3.5-4B for GAIA, SKILLER scored 43.78% versus SkillX at 44.18%, a calculated difference of -0.40 percentage points.
On Qwen3.5-4B for EarthBench, SKILLER scored 71.51% versus Manus at 71.51%, a calculated difference of +0.00 percentage points.
On Qwen3.5-9B for GAIA zero-shot split, SKILLER scored 49.59% versus AutoSkill at 47.97%, a calculated difference of +1.62 percentage points.
On Qwen3.5-9B for EarthBench zero-shot split, SKILLER scored 72.31% versus Manus at 70.43%, a calculated difference of +1.88 percentage points.
On Qwen3.5-4B for GAIA zero-shot split, SKILLER scored 40.65% versus No-skill at 34.55%, a calculated difference of +6.10 percentage points.
On Qwen3.5-4B for EarthBench zero-shot split, SKILLER scored 69.62% versus Manus at 70.97%, a calculated difference of -1.35 percentage points.

On SkillsBench, the SKILLER-generated skill profile averaged 534.33 words, TF-IDF similarity 0.07, 2.96 scripts, 15,747 lines of code, and 0.47 references per task, combining human-like low TF-IDF with the highest script count and code volume among listed methods.
Across five benchmarks on Qwen3.5-9B, SKILLER used 2.68M strong-model input tokens and 0.15M output tokens, cost $8.95, and achieved average score 62.86; SkillX cost $14.55 with average score 52.60.

State ablation on Qwen3.5-9B shows the largest degradations when removing the task instance or current trajectory: SkillsBench falls from 73.91 to 1.45 or 2.44, and SWE-Skills-Bench from 82.80 to 20.51 or 24.87.

Critic ablation shows that removing the Generation operation produces the largest loss among critic-operation ablations, with scores of 36.44 on SkillsBench, 24.90 on SWE-Skills-Bench, and 42.15 on GAIA versus 73.91, 82.80, and 49.40 for full SKILLER.

Actor ablation shows that removing helper-script synthesis reduces Qwen3.5-9B scores to 55.34 on SkillsBench and 52.30 on SWE-Skills-Bench, the strongest degradation among tested actor components on those two benchmarks.

The released SkillsBench implementation uses task-specific skill bundles and buffers, 30 tool steps per executor rollout, executor temperature 0.2, actor/critic temperature 0.3, three recent history records, bounded edits, oracle-use rejection, skill snapshots, and rollback to the most recent passing snapshot after regression.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: restores the most recent passing snapshot

atoms.canonical_statement: In the springboot-tdd qualitative example, three saved skill versions retain a seven-phase INIT-to-CONCLUDE workflow while progressively adding path/search budgets, evidence limits, interface contracts, and verifier-completion requirements.

The SWE-Skills-Bench subset is intentionally selected for tasks where adding a skill changes performance, and the paper states that its results should not be interpreted as estimates over every task in the original benchmark.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: should not be interpreted as estimates over every task

atoms.canonical_statement: The paper states that the SKILLER project is available at https://github.com/DANG-ai/SKILLER.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The project is available at https://github.com/DANG-ai/SKILLER

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors conclude that executor-specific natural-language skill optimization can let compact models outperform unoptimized models with more than twice their parameter scale on structured tasks and can provide a cost-effective agent-deployment paradigm.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: more than twice their parameter scale

atoms.canonical_statement: SkillLearnBench learning is nonmonotonic: Table 8 reports SKILLER Step 2 as the best listed checkpoint at 32.11% accuracy, while later steps retain most of the gain but do not improve on that checkpoint.
